messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Rivera was thirty when the scaffolding at the Oakridge renovation site gave way. He stood ten feet away when the planks splintered, watching Julian go down onto a rusted rebar stub. The event left him without language; it would not form into sentences for his wife or the paramedics. Instead, it lived in his body as a wordless collision of splintering timber and the exact taste of iron and chalk dust that flooded his mouth. In the weeks that followed, the past stopped feeling like a record of something that had ended. When a sudden gust carried the scent of fresh-cut wood mixed with metal, or when Elena’s hand brushed his shoulder, Mateo’s body would instantly drop back into that moment. The specific taste would return, sharp and unbidden, and he would feel the weight of splintered wood on his shoulders as if it were happening now. His days became a careful architecture of exclusion. He stopped talking about the collapse, burying any thought of the event beneath hours of work. When the images rose without warning, filling his kitchen with the visceral reality of torn flesh and frantic hands, Mateo learned to deliberately leave his body behind. He would sit at the edge of his recliner, focus on the hum of the refrigerator, and instruct his mind to go still. The strategy worked until it did not, leaving him hollowed out. To occupy the quiet spaces the blanking out carved, he turned to the pantry. He began eating excessively, finishing whole loaves and bags of chips without tasting them, using the fullness to steady his hands when the distress rose. He told himself he was managing it, but the certainty began to fray. At the job site, the world kept offering proof that something in him had broken permanently. A client’s fresh, weeping laceration on a forearm would flash across his vision and send his heart into a frantic rhythm he could not name. When his foreman clapped a heavy hand on his back to direct him toward the load-bearing wall, Mateo’s skin would prickle with the ghost of Julian’s desperate grip, and he would step back, claiming he needed to check the blueprints. His precision grew erratic. He began doubting his own judgment on every cut and measurement, certain that he could not rely on himself to keep anyone safe. The life he had built—the steady rhythm of framing, the quiet mornings with Elena—felt irrevocably shattered. He carried the heavy conviction that his life had been destroyed, that the man who understood timber was gone. The breaking point came on a Tuesday when a kitchen faucet leak left his hands stained with dark water. He stood in the doorway, paralyzed by the full sensory reliving of that collapse, unable to breathe or move or call for Elena, who had stepped into the hallway. That night, Mateo finally asked a colleague for the name of a therapist. His voice was tight with a fear that the memory would swallow him whole if he did not find a way to hold it. What he hoped for, though he could barely admit it, was not to forget the scaffolding, but to stop feeling permanently damaged by it, to trust his own hands again, and to reclaim the life he was certain had been lost.
